analysis.one_liner: Lets the labor board order pay compensation when employers unlawfully delay first contract bargaining.
analysis.headline: The bill died in a House committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers vote to form a union and an employer unlawfully refuses to bargain a first contract, the National Labor Relations Board today can order the employer to stop and post notices, but cannot make workers whole for the delay. This bill would let the Board order compensation for that delay, measured against a government statistical compilation of typical wage and benefit settlements. It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and sent to a subcommittee, where it remained until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at newly organized workplaces whose employers refuse to bargain a first contract would be able to recover pay for the time lost to an unlawful bargaining delay, turning a company's refusal to bargain from a costless stalling tactic into a paying proposition. Unions would also gain, since the remedy would make first contracts easier to reach.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the National Labor Relations Act to let the NLRB award bargaining-unit employees compensation for the delay in bargaining caused by an employer's unlawful refusal to bargain before the first contract. [S2] [S3]

Compensation would be measured by a formula comparing the wages and benefits employees actually received during the delay with the typical settlement levels tracked by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, so workers are made whole for lost raises. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers found guilty of unlawfully refusing to bargain a first contract would pay the compensation, and would lose the ability to stall a first contract indefinitely at no cost. Industries with a record of resisting first contracts would bear these costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers who unlawfully refuse to bargain

drawbacks.text: The compensation formula is rigid: it mechanically applies a Bureau of Labor Statistics settlements report to every case, which could overcompensate or undercompensate workers whose actual circumstances differ from the typical settlement data, and it depends on the continued publication of that statistical compilation. [S3]

Employers argue that a financial penalty added to bargaining disputes raises the cost of contesting a union and could push labor disputes into longer litigation before the Board, and business groups opposed stronger NLRB remedies generally. (This objection appears in general labor-policy debate, not in the provided sources.)

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: without a monetary remedy, an employer can unlawfully stall a first contract for years and the only penalty is a paperwork order, so the bill targets a well-known gap in labor law. The cost falls only on employers who violate the law, but the one-size-fits-all formula and dependence on a single BLS report make it a blunt instrument.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and then to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the bill on May 19, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day. [S1] [S5]
On June 20, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, and no further action appears in the record through the end of the 108th Congress. [S5]
The bill never gained a cosponsor. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who refuse to bargain first contracts came out ahead: the stalling tactic this bill would have made costly remains free. The measure also died without a hearing or a vote, so supporters never even got a debate on the merits.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 19, 2003, and never reported the bill or scheduled action on it; it was sent to a subcommittee on June 20 and died there. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to show how parties split; the bill's single sponsor was a Democrat and it drew no cosponsors of either party, so no meaningful coalition ever formed.

industries.industry: Employers facing new union organizing (unions' counterpart companies)
industries.note: The bill would require employers found to have unlawfully refused to bargain a first contract to pay workers compensation for the delay, ending a low-cost way to stall unionization. Its defeat leaves that stalling tactic in place.
A monetary remedy for bargaining delays makes first contracts easier to win and strengthens unions' value to members. The industry never had to engage because the bill died in committee.
